newsitem.title: GERMANY: Sceptical German press moot EMU delay.
newsitem.headline: Sceptical German press moot EMU delay.

text.p: German newspapers on Tuesday appeared weary of assurances made by finance minister Theo Waigel at his presentation of Bonn's EMU efforts in Brussels on Wednesday and of media speculation on the matter.

With Germany openly admitting it will not this year strictly meet one of the economic criteria for entry into monetary union in 1999, it would be better to accept that postponement of the project is perhaps the most sensible option, some suggested.

"A delay wouldn't mean the fall of Europe," the Munich-published Sueddeutsche Zeitung said in its editorial, adding that Germany's growing jobless levels made government economic forecasts look improbable.

"As more and more companies lay off workers, the Kohl government is relying on the hope principle. It is however highly improbable that jobless levels will fall significantly (as Bonn forecasts)"," it added.
The Handelsblatt business daily noted that Euro banknotes were not due to be in circulation until after the 1999 planned start date.

"Postponement does not mean abandonment. Distribution of the Euro banknotes is not planned before 2002, so that today there is a discussion as to whether currency conversion to the Euro needs to last a full three years..." it said.
Waigel admitted on Wednesday that Germany's debt levels would be above the 60 percent of gross domestic product strictly allowed by the Maastricht criteria for EMU entry.

But, arguing forcefully that special factors such as unification were to blame for this, Waigel stressed that Germany was doing everything to cut its running deficits to the three percent of GDP needed to meet EMU conditions.

According to the Maastricht Treaty, a country may miss the strict 60 percent debt level but still qualify if it is showing significant progresss in reaching this threshold. German debt-to-GDP is expected to stand at 61.5 percent by the end of this year.
But to the Frankfurter Rundschau the fact that it seemed possible to choose which criteria were strictly adhered to and which not was a cause for scepticism.

"Fulfilling criteria to the letter? -- yes, when it suits. 'Three percent is three percent,' Waigel says of the deficit level. But 60 percent is clearly not 60 percent when it comes to debts," it said.

For Die Welt, mounting speculation about whether EMU would be delayed or not was getting out of hand. It berated journalists for chasing headlines by continually asking EU leaders whether they could "rule out" the project.
"Even the most improbable events can never completely be ruled out. Who could rule out, for example, that Bill Clinton will not be struck down by lightning this year while out jogging?" it asked.
